newsitem.title: USA: China, US ease rules on ratites, livestock semen.
newsitem.headline: China, US ease rules on ratites, livestock semen.

text.p: U.S. and Chinese officials have signed several protocols that will improve market access for U.S. livestock and livestock genetics, the Agriculture Department said Friday.
USDA said the protocols opened China to shipments of U.S. swine semen and ratite hatching eggs. They also improve access for U.S. exports of bovine semen and ratite breeding stock.
A memorandum of understanding also was signed on avian influenza, making U.S. access for day-old chicks and hatching eggs more clear-cut and reliable, USDA said.
Ratites are heavy, flightless, three-toed birds such as ostriches and emus.

Last year, the United States exported $387 million in livestock and livestock genetics, including $6 million to China. Livestock genetics includes live chicks, hatching eggs, bovine semen and live cattle.

"With its large population and growing prosperity, China offers a market of great potential importance for U.S. producers and exporters," Terry Medley, head of the USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, said in a statement.
"That is why these protocols signal a notable step forward for U.S. livestock and livestock genetics trade."
